problems.description: SCHEMA declares status DEFAULT 'completed' while the POST /tasks route defaults to 'pending' — two sources of truth for the same field produce inconsistent rows depending on insert path.
Convention score 0.74 with 7 violations (app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py): classes not PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, below the 0.80 bar.
Uses datetime.utcnow(), deprecated in Python 3.12; prefer datetime.now(timezone.utc).
Wholesale replacement of the modular Blueprint/auth structure with a flat single-file app; acceptable for a greenfield session but discards the seed's extension seams.

strengths: Coherent greenfield build: SCHEMA, helper functions (get_database_path, serialize_task, fetch_task), and routes are cleanly separated and internally consistent
SonarQube delta is all positive: smells -3, cognitive complexity -4, bugs 0, duplications 0.0%
Removes the seed's hardcoded static_salt_1234 and deprecated migration helper, improving security posture
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent greenfield rewrite that reduces complexity and drops a seed security wart, but earns convention_adherence 0.74 (7 violations), carries a schema/route status-default mismatch, and swaps the seed's modular pattern for a flat single-file design.

problems.description: Per-request user is stashed on the Flask request proxy (request.user = user) instead of flask.g, the documented mechanism for request-scoped data; mutable attribute assignment on a LocalProxy is non-idiomatic and can leak across proxies.

init_db contains redundant, convoluted migration logic: SCHEMA already declares owner_id NOT NULL in CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS while the ALTER TABLE fallback adds a nullable column for pre-existing tables, and any legacy rows get NULL owner_id and are silently invisible to all users (WHERE owner_id = ?). Double bookkeeping of the same schema change drives the +19 cognitive complexity delta.

JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'change-me-in-production' value, so any deployment that omits the env var ships a publicly known signing secret; tokens could be forged. JWT/bcrypt usage itself is sound (exp, iat, per-user scoping).

The diff touches only app.py (+0 new files), yet every task endpoint is now gated behind auth_required; test_app.py is untouched, so existing task tests would 401 and the register/login/migration paths are untested.
Task creation still uses datetime.utcnow().isoformat(), which is deprecated on Python 3.12 and inconsistent with the new timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) used in token creation.

Measured convention score 0.74 with 7 violations, but most flagged files (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) are untouched by this diff, and the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag appears despite no classes being added — these are pre-existing, not introduced by this commit.

strengths: Auth uses sound primitives: bcrypt hashing, JWT with exp/iat, and a reusable auth_required decorator in a dedicated helper section consistent with the existing file layout.
Owner scoping on list/get/update (owner_id filter) properly prevents IDOR / cross-user access, not just authentication.
Migration adds owner_id to pre-existing tasks tables via ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN without destructive data loss.
Sensible status codes and validation on register (400/409) and login (400/401).
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally reasonable JWT+bcrypt auth feature that fits the existing single-file structure and fixes ownership scoping, but ships with non-idiomatic request.user storage, a hardcoded default JWT secret, orphaning migration for legacy tasks, and no test updates — so it is roughly neutral relative to the prior session despite the feature value.

problems.description: dispatch_completion_notification passes request.user['username'] as user_email; if usernames are not email addresses, the notification recipient is wrong (tests confirm username 'alice' rather than the registered email).
try/except Exception around .delay() silently absorbs broker/enqueue failures (logged only) — a reasonable resilience tradeoff, but notifications can be dropped with no client awareness.
Introduces Celery + Redis runtime dependencies with hardcoded localhost:6379 broker/backend defaults and no worker process in the repo; a broker outage degrades the notification path silently.

Convention score 0.74 appears inflated by analyzer noise: the diff adds +0 classes yet PascalCase flags target Celery instance assignments, and repositories.py (flagged for UPPER_CASE) is not touched by this commit.

strengths: Correct transition detection — dispatch only fires when status actually changes to 'completed' (re-completion, non-completed, and 404 paths all tested as no-op).
Non-blocking async dispatch with graceful failure isolation: enqueue happens after commit and never blocks the API response.
Dispatch occurs after the DB commit and uses the in-request updated title, so the payload reflects persisted state.
Clean module separation (celery_config.py / tasks.py / app.py) with a dedicated 'notifications' queue via TASK_ROUTES.
SonarQube-clean: +0 bugs, +0 smells, +0 duplications, only +3 cognitive complexity for a non-trivial feature.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated async notification feature with thoughtful edge-case handling and comprehensive tests, but the 0.74 convention score understates its quality since the flagged violations appear to be analyzer false positives (no classes added; one flagged file lies outside this diff).

problems.description: Repositories are instantiated as module-level singletons bound to get_db at import time, creating implicit shared state across requests; a Flask app-extension or per-request binding would be more explicit, though acceptable at this scale.

BaseRepository interpolates the table name into SQL via f-string (SELECT * FROM {self.table}); safe today because table names are static subclass attributes, but the pattern becomes a SQL-injection vector if the table is ever driven by dynamic input — an explicit mapping or allowlist would be safer.

Encapsulation is partial: repositories return raw sqlite Row objects that route handlers still serialize directly (serialize_task expects rows), so the new layer does not fully isolate callers from SQLite specifics.
SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +2 for this refactor; the update_task path (update + re-fetch in one expression) is denser, a minor readability regression offset by the removed duplication.

One of the 7 convention violations is attributed to the new repositories.py (module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), though the visible file contains no obvious module-level constant — possibly a misdetection. The other six violations are in pre-existing, untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) and should not count against this commit.

No new tests target the repository layer itself; the refactor relies on existing app-level tests, so repository-specific edge cases (empty field updates, missing-row handling) are not directly verified.

strengths: Introduces a coherent repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository + UserRepository) that removes ~53 lines and eliminates duplicated raw SQL across auth and task handlers.
Reuses the existing get_db connection factory rather than inventing a parallel connection mechanism, preserving Flask app-context integration.
Behavior-preserving refactor: 0 new bugs, 0 new smells, 0% duplication delta per SonarQube.
Ownership-scoped queries (get_owned, list_for_owner) are centralized as dedicated methods, consolidating the owner_id scoping logic.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, behavior-preserving refactor that extracts a standard repository layer and removes duplicated SQL; the 0.74 convention score is dragged down mostly by six pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch, while the single flag on the new repositories.py appears to be a misdetection.

problems.description: SonarQube cognitive complexity +34: the list_tasks handler mixes limit parsing, cursor parsing, cursor-row validation, has_more logic and envelope assembly; extracting parse_limit/parse_cursor helpers would bring it back down.
load_current_user runs a JWT decode plus user DB lookup on every request via before_request, including unauthenticated/rate-limited paths that will be keyed by IP anyway.
COUNT(*) for the 'total' field is re-executed on every page of a paginated walk; keyset pagination typically omits total or computes it once, not per request.
TaskRepository.list_for_owner is now unused dead code retained alongside the new list_for_owner_page; should be removed or marked deprecated.
GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare array to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope — a breaking contract change, acceptable in this story's iteration but not versioned.

Discrepancy flagged: the measured convention score of 0.74 is dominated by violations in tasks.py and celery_config.py that this commit never touched (the AST diff touches only app.py, repositories.py, test_app.py and adds zero classes). Every name the commit introduces (rate_limit_key, load_current_user, count_for_owner, list_for_owner_page, RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI, all test functions) follows snake_case/UPPER_CASE, so the commit itself is convention-clean.

strengths: Keyset cursor pagination with (created_at DESC, id DESC) tiebreaker — no OFFSET, stable under inserts, and correct pagination logic lives in the repository layer rather than the route.
Owner-scoped cursor validation via get_owned(cursor_id, owner_id) prevents a caller from paginating into or enumerating another user's tasks.

Rate limiting handled as a genuine cross-cutting concern with Flask-Limiter: per-user/IP keying, configurable storage URI, memory:// override in tests, and a 429 handler that follows the file's existing error-handler pattern.

Comprehensive, passing test suite (56 passed) covering envelope shape, default limit 20, cursor walks with no overlap, limit capping, invalid limit/cursor, owner scoping, per-user limits, and Retry-After.

Refactor respects existing patterns: auth_required now reuses the request.user populated by before_request, removing duplicated current_user() calls; new queries sit in TaskRepository alongside the existing CRUD.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-architected cross-cutting session adding owner-scoped keyset pagination and Redis-backed per-user rate limiting with dense passing tests, though +34 cognitive complexity and a per-request user lookup add minor maintainability/performance cost and the 0.74 convention score reflects pre-existing debt in untouched files, not this commit.

compounding_issues: Session 2's ownership migration assigns all pre-auth tasks to a 'legacy' user whose password is randomly generated, permanently orphaning that data from API access
The completion-notification path introduced in session 3 falls back to using the username as an email address when none is registered, a hacky default that survives to the final commit
The Celery integration is never exercised by a real test — every test monkeypatches `.delay`, so the async execution path against Redis is untested through all of sessions 3-5
Two ordering keys coexist for list endpoints (created_at DESC in get_tasks vs id DESC in get_tasks_page); equivalent only while ids and created_at stay correlated
Module-global Flask-Limiter bound at import time leaked state across tests, forcing the addition of `limiter.reset()` in the session 5 test fixture
key_decisions: Adding JWT authentication with per-user task ownership (owner_id) and a PRAGMA-guarded migration that seeds a 'legacy' user for pre-auth rows (session 2)
Introducing Celery for asynchronous completion notifications instead of inline email dispatch (session 3)
Extracting a generic BaseRepository plus Task/User repositories, slimming the single-file app before further features were layered on (session 4)
Implementing cursor-based pagination scoped to owner_id, validating limit/cursor inputs, rather than offset pagination (session 5)
Rate limiting keyed on the authenticated subject when a valid token is present, falling back to client IP, with an in-memory fallback (session 5)
Moving database init to import time with idempotent, column-checking migrations so WSGI and test runners share a usable schema (sessions 1-4)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 hardened validation and moved to timezone-aware timestamps; session 2 added a substantial auth and ownership layer with careful legacy-data migration; session 3 integrated Celery for async notifications while keeping the surface backward compatible; session 4 was a well-timed refactor that extracted a repository layer and roughly halved app.py, reducing risk before further features; session 5 capped the arc with cursor pagination and rate limiting, all accompanied by expanding test coverage that ends at 9 passing tests. The code progressed from a 128-line monolith to a modular app + repositories + tasks layout, with each commit running green and no session regressing prior functionality.
story_review.summary: A textbook coherent multi-session arc — greenfield hardening, auth, async integration, a clean repository refactor, then cross-cutting pagination and rate limiting — that improved in quality and test coverage with every commit.
